explication:
<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   - Planka is a full-stack, open-source project‐tracking (Kanban) application.  
   - It has a React/Redux front end (“client/”), a Sails.js REST & WebSocket back end (“server/”), and a PostgreSQL database.  
   - It supports real-time updates (socket.io), file storage (local FS or S3), OIDC single-sign-on, notifications (email, Slack, Telegram, Google Chat, Webhooks), and can be deployed via Docker, Docker Compose, or Helm/Kubernetes.

2. Analyze the file structure  
   - Top-level:  
     • client/ – React/Redux UI  
     • server/ – Sails.js API & business logic  
     • config/ – Docker, nginx, development configs  
     • charts/ – Helm chart for Kubernetes  
     • docker-compose*.yml – local dev and production orchestration  
     • Dockerfile(.base) – Docker images  
   - Patterns & frameworks:  
     • Front end: Redux-Saga for side effects, Redux-ORM for models, react-beautiful-dnd for drag-and-drop  
     • Back end: Sails.js MVC (controllers, models, helpers), Knex.js for migrations/seeds  
     • WebSockets: Sails sockets for real-time updates  
     • Hooks & policies: Sails lifecycle hooks for current user, file manager (Local/S3), OIDC, SMTP, S3, watcher  
     • External services: OIDC provider, email/notification services, file storage

3. Extract architecture details from README  
   - Tech stack: React, Redux, Redux-Saga, Redux-ORM, Semantic UI React, react-beautiful-dnd; Sails.js, Knex.js; PostgreSQL  
   - Features: Projects → Boards → Lists → Cards → Tasks, attachments, comments, due dates, time tracking, notifications, SSO

4. Main components and their interactions  
   a. User’s Browser (React client)  
      • Sends HTTP(S) REST requests to the Sails.js API  
      • Establishes a WebSocket (socket.io) connection for real-time events  
      • Interacts with Redux store, sagas, ORM models  
   b. Sails.js API Server  
      • Exposes REST endpoints (controllers in server/api/controllers/)  
      • Manages authentication & policies (is-authenticated, is-admin)  
      • Broadcasts events via WebSockets  
      • Orchestrates business logic in helpers and hooks  
      • Uses Knex.js to run database queries & migrations  
      • Stores uploaded files locally or to S3 via file-manager hook  
      • Sends outbound notifications (email, Slack, Telegram, Google Chat, Webhooks)  
      • Performs OIDC single-sign-on (exchange, token handling)  
   c. PostgreSQL Database  
      • Schemas defined by Knex migrations (server/db/migrations/)  
      • Data models (server/api/models and client/src/models mirror)  
   d. File Storage  
      • Local filesystem under server/private or S3 bucket  
   e. External Identity Provider (OIDC)  
      • For SSO login/exchange  
   f. Notification Services  
      • SMTP, Slack, Telegram, Google Chat, Webhooks  
   g. Deployment & Infrastructure  
      • Docker images (Dockerfile, Dockerfile.base)  
      • Docker Compose for dev & staging  
      • Helm chart (charts/planka/) for Kubernetes  
      • Healthcheck script, start.sh entrypoint  
      • CI/CD workflows (.github/workflows/) build, push, test, release  

5. Architectural patterns & design principles  
   - Clear separation of concerns: UI ↔ API ↔ Persistence  
   - MVC on the server, modular controllers & helpers  
   - Redux-Saga for side-effects & async flows on the client  
   - Redux-ORM for normalized client models  
   - WebSocket pub/sub for real-time synchronization  
   - Pluggable hooks for file management & authentication  
   - Infrastructure as code via Docker & Helm  

6. Guidelines for tailoring your diagram  
   - Partition the diagram into lanes or tiers:  
     • Client tier (React app)  
     • API tier (Sails.js server + websockets)  
     • Data tier (PostgreSQL + file storage)  
     • External services tier (OIDC, email, messaging)  
     • Deployment tier (Docker/Helm/Kubernetes)  
   - Use containers (boxes) to represent each logical service  
   - Show inbound/outbound protocols: HTTP(S), WebSocket, S3 API, SMTP, REST calls to OIDC and webhook targets  

7. Diagramming instructions  
   - Label each component clearly (e.g., “React Client”, “Sails.js API”, “PostgreSQL DB”, “S3 Bucket”, “OIDC Provider”)  
   - Use directional arrows showing:  
     • Client → API (REST calls)  
     • Client ↔ API (WebSocket)  
     • API → DB (SQL)  
     • API → File Storage (S3 or FS)  
     • API → External Services (SMTP, Slack, Webhooks, OIDC)  
   - Color-code by tier:  
     • Front end (blue)  
     • Back end (green)  
     • Persistence (orange)  
     • External (purple)  
     • Deployment (gray)  
   - Use different shapes for:  
     • Processes (circles/rounded rectangles)  
     • Datastores (cylinders)  
     • External systems (cloud icons)  
   - Annotate any critical configurations:  
     • OIDC token flow (exchange & verify)  
     • Authentication cookie handling (HTTP-only tokens)  
     • WebSocket authorization  

8. Be comprehensive  
   - Capture every key element: UI modules, API controllers, DB migrations, hooks, external integrations, deployment configs  
   - Don’t worry about drawing every single file—focus on logical groupings (e.g., “Controllers”, “Helpers”, “Policies”).  
   - Provide enough detail so a new engineer can understand data flow, integration points, and deployment topology at a glance.  
   - Keep the diagram readable: group related elements into bounded boxes and use clear legend for colors/shapes.
</explanation>
